question: The third fire in a recycling plant in a year broke out in Thessaloniki, while the fire that started in the landfill on Paros was devastating. This unacceptable situation is a direct consequence of EU policy, which serves the profitability of business groups that make a fortune from waste. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that destructive fires are constantly breaking out in landfills, as well as yet another in a recycling plant, given that the necessary protective measures to prevent fires or other natural disasters, with the necessary personnel and infrastructure, are not being observed, while these plants operate near residential areas, creating additional risks of pollution and contamination?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that there is an urgent need to fund epidemiological studies and imaging tests on the population for cancers, respiratory and other diseases, so that there is a thorough investigation of the consequences on the health and life of the residents of the areas adjacent to these units, as well as in the wider region?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the ‘green’ declarations of the EU, such as Directive (EU) 2024/2881 and Directive 2006/118/EC, and those of governments, are proven not to be aimed at protecting the environment, but on the contrary legitimise this unacceptable situation, as, among other things, no substantive measures are being taken and there is no established mechanism for the immediate restoration of polluted land in order to avoid contamination of the aquifer, the groundwater of the area and the air?
answer: Environmental and health risks from fires at recycling plants (1) and landfills (2) are prevented by EU law on permitting and monitoring, consideration of distances from landfills to residential areas and prevention of fire hazards (3). Member States shall ensure that EU law is correctly implemented, and if necessary, impose sanctions. The EU funds research and innovation on hazardous waste and air pollution.

The ExpoHealthNet (4) projects study the role of such pollution in non-communicable diseases and inform public health policy (5). The European Cancer Inequalities Registry (6) monitors disparities in cancer burden, prevention and care across Member States. Its Data Tool provides cancer indicators, including environmental cancer risk factors.

The Country Cancer Profiles (7) examine the national situation regarding exposure to air pollution, and other environmental and occupational carcinogens. Directive (EU) 2024/2881 (8) requires Member States to ensure that air quality meets EU-wide standards and take measures to achieve those objectives.

Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives, OJ L 312, 22.11.2008, p. 3-30, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/851 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May, OJ L 150, 14.6.2018, p. 109-140 and Directive (EU) 2025/1892 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 September 2025, OJ L, 2025/1892, 26.9.2025.

Council Directive 1999/31/EC of 26 April 1999 on the landfill of waste, OJ L 182, 16.7.1999, p. 1-19, amended by Directive (EU) 2018/850 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 2018, OJ L 150, 14.6.2018, p. 100-108. Annex I, Section 1-5 to Directive 1999/31/EC.

ExpoHealthNet (2025-2029) received a funding of EUR 57 million and consists of 7 projects connecting more than 100 organisations from 29 countries: https://expohealthnet.eu/. Other relevant R&I projects study indoor air quality in various settings, The Indoor Air and Health Cluster: https://www.idealcluster.

eu/, urban air quality and health, EXPANSE project of the European Human Exposome Network (EHEN): https://expanseproject.eu/, and the socioeconomic costs of (air) pollution, Cluster for Methods for assessing health-related costs of environmental stressors (METEOR): https://meteor-research.eu/.

In 2025 the Commission launched a EUR 40 million call aiming to further elucidate the impact of pollution on brain diseases and disorders, https://ec.europa.eu/info/fundingtenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-HLTH-2025-03-ENVHLTH-01-two-stage. https://cancer-inequalities.jrc.ec.europa.eu/. https://cancer-inequalities.jrc.ec.europa.eu/country-cancer-profiles-2025.
Directive (EU) 2024/2881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe (recast), OJ L, 2024/2881, 20.11.

2024, the ‘Ambient Air Quality Directive’,, also Annex I to Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 November 2010 on industrial and livestock rearing emissions (integrated pollution prevention and control) (Recast), OJ L 334, 17.12.2010, p. 17-119, as amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1785 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 OJ L, 15.7.2024.

Fires at recycling plants and landfills are not exempted. If alert or information thresholds are exceeded or forecast, the public must be informed immediately. Directive 2006/118/EC requires Member States to ensure the good chemical status of groundwater bodies and take action to prevent deterioration of the status, including by measures to prevent and control groundwater pollution (9).

Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, pp. 1-73; Directive 2006/118/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 on the protection of groundwater against pollution and deterioration, OJ L 372, 27.12.2006, p. 19-31.
